sections.h2: Who runs property tax in Monroe County, Kentucky?
sections.html:
Monroe County property tax runs through the courthouse at 200 North Main Street in Tompkinsville. The PVA (Property Valuation Administrator) assesses homes, the sheriff collects the bill, and the county clerk handles delinquent tax bills and liens. The county attorney, in a separate office on North Main Street, arranges payment plans.

This is the Kentucky Monroe County, in the Eastern Pennyroyal Plateau.

sections.h2: What is Monroe County like for a house seller?
sections.html:
Monroe County covers about 329 square miles of land on the Tennessee line and was formed in 1820, named for President James Monroe. Tompkinsville, the seat, took its name from his vice president, Daniel Tompkins, and Wikipedia notes no other county named for a president has a seat named for that president's vice president. Fountain Run and Gamaliel are the other cities. Neighbors are Barren, Metcalfe, Cumberland and Allen counties, plus Clay and Macon counties in Tennessee.

The county website describes the Upper Cumberland hills, the Cumberland River and the headwaters of the Barren River. History is visible on the ground: the Old Mulkey Meetinghouse State Historic Site holds the oldest log meetinghouse in Kentucky, built in 1804, on a 20 acre park. Confederate raiders under John Hunt Morgan attacked a Union garrison here on July 9, 1862.

Monroe County was a dry county until voters approved alcohol sales on November 7, 2023, according to Wikipedia.

sections.h2: What do Census numbers show for Monroe County housing?
sections.html:
Monroe County is the only one of these four counties that has lost people since 2020. The Census Bureau counted 11,338 that year, up from 10,963 in 2010, and its 2025 estimate is 11,191, a 1.3 percent decline. The county holds 5,300 housing units.

The 2020 to 2024 survey adds the following:

  • Owners live in 70.9 percent of homes, the lowest share of the four counties, so rentals are a bigger part of the market.
  • Median owner costs are $1,056 with a mortgage and $397 without.
  • Broadband subscriptions reach 83.9 percent of households.
  • The mean commute is 28.4 minutes.
  • Total employment was 2,649 in 2023, down 1.9 percent from 2022.

sections.h2: Which Monroe County offices should you call or visit?
sections.html:
The county's officials page lists the courthouse suites below, all in Tompkinsville, KY 42167.

  • Sheriff: tax collection. 200 North Main Street, Suite E, phone (270) 487-6622.
  • PVA: assessments and exemptions. 200 North Main Street, Suite A, phone (270) 487-6401.
  • County Clerk: delinquent bills and liens. 200 North Main Street, Suite D, phone (270) 487-5471.
  • County Attorney: 215 North Main Street, phone (270) 487-6303.

The clerk's delinquent tax page also says a bill sold at the tax sale may carry a third party's costs, so find out first whether your certificate has been sold.

sections.h2: What is the Monroe County delinquent tax sale?
sections.html:
After April 15 each year, the clerk creates a certificate of delinquency, which is a lien of record on the property. The clerk's page says certificates are created on or about April 16. Interest grows every month, so paying early costs less.

The clerk set the 2026 sale for September 23, 2026 at 1:00 p.m. Central in the clerk's office, and that date has passed. A certificate that goes unpaid at the sale may be bought by a private party, and the buyer can add substantial administrative costs. Collection by the county attorney or a buyer may include foreclosure.

  • Payment by mail: money order only.
  • Payment in person: check, cash or credit card, with possible card fees.
  • Payment plan: ask the County Attorney's office, but plans end once a bill is sold.

The page lists the clerk's phone number for checking whether your certificate has been bought and who bought it.

sections.h2: When are regular Monroe County bills due?
sections.html:
Until April 15, you pay the sheriff on the state calendar in KRS 134.015. Bills are mailed in the fall, a 2 percent discount applies through November 1, and the face amount is due by December 31.

A 5 percent penalty applies during January, and a 10 percent penalty applies after January 31. The Department of Revenue states the combined penalty as 21 percent for February 1 through April 15,. Its example turns a $1,000 bill into a $1,254 certificate at the clerk's office, and once it reaches the clerk, that bill totals $1,387.79 if paid within five business days.

sections.h2: How do you dispute a Monroe County assessment?
sections.html:
You begin with a PVA conference, which the state requires before an owner can file. The roll is open starting the first Monday in May for about two weeks, and you must file at the clerk's office by the following workday after it closes.

When you file, you name your own opinion of value. If bills go out before the appeal ends and the final value lands above your claim, you receive a supplemental bill for the difference. The board then meets 25 to 35 days after the window and can sit five days. Bring the evidence the Department of Revenue lists: the land and building details, insurance policies, construction costs and sales listings.

sections.h2: How are rural parcels valued in Monroe County?
sections.html:
With about 329 square miles and 34.4 people per square mile, Monroe County has many sales with land attached. The Department of Revenue requires the PVA to inspect every parcel at least once every four years and to add new construction each year. Farm land may be assessed at agricultural value instead of fair cash value, so ask the PVA how your acreage is classified before you list it.

Parcels near the Tennessee line, along the river or in the hills can differ widely in value. If the roll lists a building that has been torn down or a barn that has been added, ask for a correction at a PVA conference.

sections.h2: How does the homestead exemption work in Monroe County?
sections.html:
It is open to owners who are 65 or older, or totally disabled, who live in the house. Apply at the Monroe County PVA with proof, and use the form the state prescribes.

KRS 132.810 sets one exemption per unit, even when the owner is both 65 and disabled or several residents are 65 or older. The figure moves with a federal price index every two years when it shifts at least 1 percent. If you sell or the owner dies, the transfer has to be reported to the PVA.

sections.h2: Can you sell a Monroe County house that owes tax?
sections.html:
Yes, and the usual path is to get a payoff in writing. Before April 15, the sheriff gives it. After that date, the clerk gives it, and the figure rises each month and includes the clerk and attorney fees.

Tax ownership is set on January 1, and the tax is the personal debt of the person who owned then, under KRS 134.015. The lien can follow the property for 11 years. Houses in Monroe County that need work, or that heirs inherited, often change hands with a bill still open, so build the payoff into your numbers when you compare a listing with a cash sale.

faqs.q: Where do I pay Monroe County property tax?
faqs.a: Pay the Monroe County Sheriff at 200 North Main Street, Suite E, Tompkinsville. The office phone is (270) 487-6622.

faqs.q: When was the Monroe County tax sale in 2026?
faqs.a: The clerk scheduled it for September 23, 2026 at 1:00 p.m. Central. Call the clerk at (270) 487-5471 to learn whether a certificate was sold.

faqs.q: Can I set up a payment plan on a delinquent Monroe County bill?
faqs.a: Yes, through the County Attorney's office, if the certificate has not been sold at the tax sale. Plans are not available after a sale.

faqs.q: How can I pay the clerk by mail?
faqs.a: By money order only. The clerk accepts check, cash and credit card for in person payments.

faqs.q: What is the Monroe County PVA phone number?
faqs.a: The PVA office is at 200 North Main Street, Suite A in Tompkinsville, and the phone is (270) 487-6401.
